stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe, crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm. His ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Based on his clinical presentation and ECG findings, which of the following best describes the mechanism of his myocardial infarction?
stemHtml: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset, severe, crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm. His ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Based on his clinical presentation and ECG findings, which of the following best describes the mechanism of his myocardial infarction? (Question Id: 502121)
options: Transmural myocardial necrosis due to complete coronary artery occlusion
Subendocardial ischemia due to partial obstruction
optionsHtml: Transmural myocardial necrosis due to complete coronary artery occlusion
keywords: “Crushing chest pain” – Classic symptom of acute myocardial infarction.
“ST-segment elevation in II, III, aVF” – Indicates inferior wall STEMI caused by complete coronary artery occlusion.
keywordsHtml: 1. “Crushing chest pain” – Classic symptom of acute myocardial infarction.
1. “ST-segment elevation in II, III, aVF” – Indicates inferior wall STEMI caused by complete coronary artery occlusion.

A.title: Transmural myocardial necrosis due to complete coronary artery occlusion
A.body:
The patient's presentation—sudden-onset, severe, crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm—is a classic sign of an acute myocardial infarction (MI).
The key diagnostic finding is the ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF on the ECG.
ST-segment elevation on an ECG signifies a STEMI (ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction). This pattern indicates a full-thickness (or transmural) injury to the heart muscle caused by a prolonged, complete occlusion of a major coronary artery, most commonly due to a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque leading to a thrombus (blood clot) completely blocking the vessel. Leads II, III, and aVF look at the inferior wall of the heart, meaning the infarction is likely due to the blockage of the Right Coronary Artery (RCA).
The resulting lack of blood flow (ischemia) is severe and prolonged enough to cause transmural myocardial necrosis (death of the heart muscle across the entire wall thickness).
Early intervention (PCI or thrombolysis) is critical to limit myocardial damage.
A.bodyHtml:
• The patient's presentation—sudden-onset, severe, crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm—is a classic sign of an acute myocardial infarction (MI).
  • The key diagnostic finding is the ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF on the ECG.
  • ST-segment elevation on an ECG signifies a STEMI (ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction). This pattern indicates a full-thickness (or transmural) injury to the heart muscle caused by a prolonged, complete occlusion of a major coronary artery, most commonly due to a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque leading to a thrombus (blood clot) completely blocking the vessel. Leads II, III, and aVF look at the inferior wall of the heart, meaning the infarction is likely due to the blockage of the Right Coronary Artery (RCA).
  • The resulting lack of blood flow (ischemia) is severe and prolonged enough to cause transmural myocardial necrosis (death of the heart muscle across the entire wall thickness).
  • Early intervention (PCI or thrombolysis) is critical to limit myocardial damage.

B.title: Subendocardial ischemia due to partial obstruction
B.body:
Causes NSTEMI, not STEMI.
ECG shows ST-segment depression or T-wave inversion, not elevation.
Ischemia is limited to the inner layer (subendocardium), not full-thickness.
B.bodyHtml:
• Causes NSTEMI, not STEMI.
  • ECG shows ST-segment depression or T-wave inversion, not elevation.
  • Ischemia is limited to the inner layer (subendocardium), not full-thickness.

C.title: Vasospasm with no plaque rupture
C.body:
Seen in Prinzmetal/variant angina, usually transient ST elevation.
Pain often occurs at rest, often nocturnal, and resolves spontaneously or with nitrates.
Usually not associated with complete infarction unless prolonged.
C.bodyHtml:
• Seen in Prinzmetal/variant angina, usually transient ST elevation.
  • Pain often occurs at rest, often nocturnal, and resolves spontaneously or with nitrates.
  • Usually not associated with complete infarction unless prolonged.

D.title: Myocardial inflammation without infarction
D.body:
Suggests myocarditis, which may show diffuse ST changes and elevated troponins.
Pain is usually less typical, may be pleuritic, not classic crushing chest pain.
No localized coronary occlusion.
D.bodyHtml:
• Suggests myocarditis, which may show diffuse ST changes and elevated troponins.
  • Pain is usually less typical, may be pleuritic, not classic crushing chest pain.
  • No localized coronary occlusion.

E.title: Microvascular disease only
E.body:
Seen in small-vessel disease or cardiac syndrome X.
ECG changes are usually minimal or absent; ST elevation is uncommon.
Chest pain is often exertional, not acute STEMI pattern.
E.bodyHtml:
• Seen in small-vessel disease or cardiac syndrome X.
  • ECG changes are usually minimal or absent; ST elevation is uncommon.
  • Chest pain is often exertional, not acute STEMI pattern.

keyConcept: Inferior STEMI with ST elevation in II, III, aVF is caused by complete occlusion of the RCA, leading to transmural myocardial necrosis. NSTEMI, vasospasm, myocarditis, and microvascular disease present differently on ECG and clinical features.
keyConceptHtml: Inferior STEMI with ST elevation in II, III, aVF is caused by complete occlusion of the RCA, leading to transmural myocardial necrosis. NSTEMI, vasospasm, myocarditis, and microvascular disease present differently on ECG and clinical features.

diagram.name: NSTEMI (Non–ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction)
diagram.caption: This diagram illustrates the pathophysiology, clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and management of NSTEMI. It highlights partial coronary artery occlusion leading to subendocardial ischemia, presenting with chest pain and elevated troponin without ST-segment elevation, and outlines key treatment strategies including antiplatelets, anticoagulation, and early invasive intervention.
diagram.captionHtml: This diagram illustrates the pathophysiology, clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and management of NSTEMI. It highlights partial coronary artery occlusion leading to subendocardial ischemia, presenting with chest pain and elevated troponin without ST-segment elevation, and outlines key treatment strategies including antiplatelets, anticoagulation, and early invasive intervention.
